title: Nepal's Disaster Demands a Regional Response
gist: Foreign Policy's South Asia Brief argues Nepal's catastrophic glacier-collapse flood should push Himalayan neighbors toward using existing regional bodies (ICIMOD) and the Indus Waters Treaty's information-sharing template for transboundary disaster monitoring, alongside a week's other South Asia news: a 400-strong Xi Jinping delegation heading to India, a Hague ruling against India on the Indus Waters Treaty, and the RSS's US image-rehabilitation push.

insights.claim: Nepal's late-August 2026 flooding, triggered by a glacier collapse and landslide along the border with Tibet, has killed more than 1,100 people with nearly 4,000 still missing, making it Nepal's deadliest natural disaster since the 2015 earthquake that killed nearly 9,000.
insights.speaker: Michael Kugelman
insights.so_what: Sets scale context for reconstruction aid flows and insurance/reinsurance exposure in the Himalayan region.
insights.locator: A week after catastrophic flooding in Nepal

insights.claim: Nepal's reformist government, in office since March after the ouster of the previous administration, initially declined offers of foreign search-and-rescue assistance after the flood but quickly reversed course.
insights.speaker: Michael Kugelman
insights.so_what: Signals early instability/inexperience in the new government's crisis-response instincts, worth watching in how it handles future foreign-aid negotiations.
insights.locator: Kathmandu initially declined offers of assistance

themes.theme: Existing institutions as a cooperation template

insights.claim: Nepal hosts the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD), a regional body spanning the eight Hindu Kush Himalaya states — including India, Pakistan, and China — that has already launched a coordinated regional glacier-monitoring strategy and developed community-level flood warning systems, despite its fractious membership.
insights.speaker: Michael Kugelman
insights.so_what: ICIMOD is the existing institutional vehicle to watch for any post-disaster expansion of transboundary glacier/flood monitoring funding or mandate.
insights.locator: an effective regional organization that can provide an institutional mechanism

insights.claim: The author proposes the Indus Waters Treaty's information-sharing model — in which commissioners from India and Pakistan meet periodically to exchange hydrological data — as a template that Nepal, China, India, and other Himalayan neighbors could adapt to monitor early-warning signs of glacier-collapse disasters like the one that hit Nepal.
insights.speaker: Michael Kugelman
insights.so_what: A concrete institutional template that, if adopted, would materially reduce future glacier-disaster tail risk in the Himalayan region — worth watching for diplomatic follow-through in coming months.
insights.locator: There is also a regional success story that Nepal can look to

insights.claim: A Stimson Center senior fellow who studies Nepal's disasters argues that greater communication and collaborative analysis of transboundary risks between Nepal and China are urgently needed.
insights.speaker: Michael Kugelman
insights.so_what: Independent expert corroboration that current Nepal-China disaster-risk coordination is inadequate, reinforcing the case for new bilateral or ICIMOD-based mechanisms.
insights.quote: greater communication, information sharing, and collaborative analysis of transboundary risks between Nepal and China are sorely needed
insights.locator: As Stimson Center senior fellow Austin Lord

themes.theme: China-India thaw ahead of Xi's visit

insights.claim: Xi Jinping will visit India for the first time since 2019 to attend a BRICS summit on Sept. 12-13, bringing a delegation of around 400 people — roughly twice the size of his 2019 delegation.
insights.speaker: Michael Kugelman
insights.so_what: Delegation size is a proxy for the scale of trade/investment scouting activity to expect; watch for announcements of Chinese commercial deals with India around the summit dates.
insights.locator: Xi to visit India with 400-strong delegation.

insights.claim: India-China relations plunged into crisis after the 2020 Ladakh border clash but began recovering from 2024 following a new border agreement and pledges to strengthen commercial cooperation, with both countries now incentivized to hedge against U.S. tariff policy and unpredictability under Trump's second term.
insights.speaker: Michael Kugelman
insights.so_what: US tariff unpredictability is functioning as an accelerant for India-China commercial rapprochement — a second-order geopolitical effect of Trump trade policy worth pricing into India-China trade-flow forecasts.
insights.locator: the two sides have bounced back

themes.theme: Indus Waters Treaty under legal strain

insights.claim: The Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague ruled that India must uphold its obligations under the Indus Waters Treaty, including on two disputed dam-building projects, rejecting India's suspension of the treaty that followed the April 2025 Kashmir terrorist attack.
insights.speaker: Michael Kugelman
insights.so_what: India's rejection of the ruling signals continued erosion of a treaty long cited as a rare durable India-Pakistan cooperation mechanism — a risk factor for transboundary water/hydropower project financing in the basin.
insights.locator: A ruling against India on the IWT.

insights.claim: India rejected the arbitration court's ruling, arguing a neutral expert was already reviewing the disputed dam cases and that the court therefore had no standing to weigh in — complicated by the World Bank (the treaty's co-signer) having simultaneously appointed both a neutral expert and an arbitration court chair.
insights.speaker: Michael Kugelman
insights.so_what: A procedural conflict at the World Bank level is now compounding the treaty's dispute-resolution breakdown, raising the odds of a prolonged, unresolved India-Pakistan water dispute.
insights.locator: India rejected the court's decision this week

themes.theme: RSS image rehabilitation in the US

insights.claim: RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat spoke at a Madison Square Garden 'interfaith gathering' event over the weekend, professing support for religious tolerance, while hundreds protested and NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani called the RSS 'exclusionary'; the RSS has recently hired lobbyists in Washington as part of a broader effort to project a more mainstream global image.
insights.speaker: Michael Kugelman
insights.so_what: A US lobbying and image campaign by a Hindu nationalist organization closely tied to India's ruling party is a soft-power/political-risk data point relevant to US-India relations and diaspora political dynamics.
insights.quote: if any Hindu thinks that there should be no Muslims in India, he will not remain Hindu
insights.locator: RSS chief attends event in New York.

insights.claim: The fifth anniversary of the U.S. withdrawal from Afghanistan passed with little attention; the Trump administration's objectives there are now limited essentially to securing the release of U.S. captives, even as Taliban leaders pitch the U.S. on investing in the country's critical minerals.
insights.speaker: Michael Kugelman
insights.so_what: Despite the Trump administration's general openness to commercial opportunities abroad, the author argues the Taliban's critical-minerals investment pitch will be a hard sell given Washington's desire to keep distance from the sanctioned leadership — a signal that Afghan minerals remain effectively closed to major Western capital for now.
insights.locator: In recent days, Taliban leaders have made pitches
